summary: AstroMission is an interactive space mission design game that allows users to experience the challenges of planning a space exploration mission. Players can select a destination, choose spacecraft and scientific instruments, and manage important resources such as fuel, power, mass and budget. The game demonstrates how engineering decisions affect mission success. It aims to make space exploration and mission planning easier to understand through an engaging and educational simulation. By combining game-based learning with space science concepts, AstroMission encourages students to explore the technologies and decisions involved in real-world space missions.
details:
AstroMission is an interactive space mission design game. Players choose a destination (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune or Pluto), a mission type (flyby, orbiter or lander), a spacecraft bus, launch vehicle, power system, propulsion and science instruments. Live meters show budget, launch mass, power, delta-v and flight time. When every check passes, the player launches and watches the transfer orbit, and each mission phase (launch, cruise, course correction, arrival, operations) succeeds or fails based on the design's margins.

How it works: the game uses NASA Planetary Fact Sheet values (mass, diameter, gravity, escape velocity, distance from the Sun, orbital period and velocity). From these it calculates Hohmann transfer delta-v and flight time, propellant mass with the rocket equation, and solar power with the inverse-square law using the 1361 W/m2 solar constant. Budget tiers and the power and instrument classes are modelled on NASA's Europa Clipper (about $5.2 billion, 9 science instruments) and Mars 2020 (about $2.4 billion, 110 W radioisotope power, 7 instruments).

Benefits and impact: students and teachers can feel why real missions need more fuel, power and money as targets get farther away, without needing equations. We hope to make mission planning approachable and inspire interest in space careers.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single page with canvas animation) and Google Fonts. The code, interface and visuals were generated with an SI tool (Claude, by Anthropic) from our own game concept and design brief, and are labelled as SI-generated in the game (canvas watermark, footer and page metadata).

Creativity: gravity-assist and electric-propulsion trade-offs, three real-budget tiers, and a success chance for every mission phase based on the player's margins.

Limitations: calculations are simplified (patched conics, Hohmann transfers). Instrument masses, power and costs are game-balanced estimates, not real instrument specifications.
